papers.title: Spectral envelopes of facial movements predict intention, cortical representations, and neural prosthetic control.
papers.abstract: Animals use coordinated facial movements to sample the environment, ingest nutrients, and communicate. Rodents produce rhythmic facial movements during spontaneous behavior and cognitive tasks. Measuring these movements precisely and linking them to neural activity remains challenging. We introduce face-rhythm, an unsupervised pipeline that combines markerless point-tracking, spectral analysis, and non-negative tensor decomposition to reduce facial video to a small set of interpretable components. Applied to videos of mice performing Pavlovian conditioning, a brain-machine interface task, and free behavior, face-rhythm recovers whisking, sniffing, licking, and subtler motifs. The resulting components are consistent across animals, decode task variables and internal states, and explain cortical activity with a low-rank representation. Facial motor cortex neurons are predicted well by a phase-invariant spectral transformation of movements above roughly 0.5 Hz, whereas slower movements retain a phase-variant representation. Face-rhythm compares favorably with deep-learning tracking and embedding methods while yielding an interpretable description of facial behavior.

papers.title: Cortical and meningeal neuroimmune interactions contribute to the generation of migraine headaches.
papers.abstract: Migraine is a prevalent disorder that ranks as the second leading cause of disability among all diseases. Recent advancements have significantly enhanced our comprehension of its underlying pathophysiology. Growing evidence highlights complex neuroimmune signaling networks-particularly interactions between meningeal nociceptors and resident immune cells-as key contributors to headache generation. The clinical success of anti-calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) antibodies underscores the importance of intercellular communication between the dural nociceptive nerves and adjacent resident immune cells such as macrophages in migraine headache. Notably, the intercellular inflammatory interplay is not confined to the meninges. Disturbances within the brain parenchyma potentially act as initiating triggers, as suggested by the presence of aura and premonitory symptoms preceding the headache. Recent experimental discoveries indicate that neuronal stress triggers an inflammatory signaling cascade that, through interactions with astrocytes and microglia, propagates to the meninges, ultimately inducing meningeal neurogenic inflammation and headache. This model is supported by converging experimental evidence and human imaging studies employing PET and quantitative MRI, which document the presence of changes compatible with inflammatory activity within the brain parenchyma and overlying meninges of patients with migraine with aura. Genetic studies identifying several inflammation-related genes and pathways as risk factors for migraine further corroborate this concept. Furthermore, cell-specific transcriptomic analyses of mouse brains have revealed astrocyte-selective activation of nuclear factor kappa B -regulated inflammatory transcriptional pathways after cortical spreading depolarization, the neurophysiological correlate of migraine aura. Owing to their extensive interface with the cerebrospinal fluid, astrocytes are uniquely positioned to release inflammatory mediators to activate meningeal nociceptors and immune cells. Insights from pain research suggest that neuroimmune interactions may be responsible for the widespread parenchymal increases in 18 kDa translocator protein (TSPO) PET signals observed in migraine with aura patients. This discovery also identifies TSPO as a potential player in migraine pathophysiology and novel drug target. In this review, by integrating cellular and molecular findings from peripheral pain and inflammation research, we examine the dynamic interactions between neurons and glia, as well as between meningeal nociceptors and immune cells in the context of migraine headache. This perspective provides a conceptual framework for understanding how nociceptors and glial cells coordinate to signal non-homeostatic brain states-initiating protective, tightly regulated responses without progressing to overt neuroinflammatory disease and provides novel insight into the findings of PET studies involving TSPO.

papers.title: The neural mechanisms of fast versus slow decision-making.
papers.abstract: One hallmark of intelligent behavior is the ability to optimize how much time is devoted to decisions. Yet the principles governing decision timing remain unclear. Here, we developed a novel paradigm for directly comparing decision-making between mice and humans. This approach allowed us to combine widefield and 2-photon imaging in the mouse frontal cortex with optogenetic inhibition to examine the underlying mechanisms. We found that history-dependent refinement of sequences in the medial frontal cortex (MFC), versus a thresholding mechanism in the lateral frontal cortex (LFC), provides a unified logic for decision strategy on a trial-by-trial basis. Notably, behavioral performance and strategy were profoundly disrupted by optogenetic inhibition of the MFC compared with that of the LFC, revealing a dominant cognitive role for MFC in decision selection and timing. These dynamics reflect reinforcement-learning updates that explain timing variability better than sensory evidence. Our findings provide a computational framework that unifies voluntary decision-making across species.

papers.title: ERN EURO-NMD expert opinion on management of new biologic therapies in myasthenia gravis.
papers.abstract: Myasthenia Gravis is a potentially life-threatening autoimmune disease of the neuromuscular junction with fluctuating muscle weakness and fatigability. In recent years, the therapeutic landscape has been notably reshaped by the introduction of new therapies. These agents, primarily acting through complement inhibition or neonatal Fc-receptor blockade, have demonstrated significant efficacy and favorable safety profiles in randomized clinical trials and real-world settings. Their advent has refined clinical management, particularly in refractory patients, leading to meaningful improvements in patients' quality of life and future expectations. Meanwhile, in this evolving therapeutic landscape, new challenges and uncertainties in clinical decision-making have been raised, as new therapies are now part of the standard care in Myasthenia Gravis. Differences in regulatory agency approvals and reimbursement policies across Europe result in heterogeneous access to therapies, complicating treatment decisions and limiting shared real-world experiences. Consequently, clinicians face complex dilemmas regarding optimal patient selection, treatment choice, and long-term management strategies. To address these issues, a panel of experts, including adult and pediatric neurologists and patient representatives, within the framework of the European Reference Network for Neuromuscular Diseases convened to develop consensus-based positions. The aim of this work was to identify, explore, and discuss key challenges associated with the use of new therapies and to propose a practical approach to support clinicians in this rapidly evolving field. Given the variability in clinical approach, treatment availability and reimbursement policies across European healthcare systems, this position paper seeks to provide guidance that are adaptable across diverse settings. A literature review was conducted, focusing on pivotal clinical trials and real-world evidence. Eleven key topics were identified and discussed, and for each, consensus statements were developed and refined through a modified Delphi process: patient assessment from both clinician and patient perspectives; the role of autoantibodies and optimization of serological testing; selection of immunotherapies; definitions of treatment response and failure in the context of new therapies; strategies for switching between therapies; predictors of treatment response; management of concomitant therapies, including corticosteroids and conventional immunosuppressant; discontinuation strategies; their potential role as early-line therapies; their applicability in ocular MG; and future therapeutic perspectives, including ongoing clinical trials. In conclusion, new therapies represent a major advance in Myasthenia Gravis care but also introduce significant complexity. This expert position paper provides a framework to support clinicians in decision-making and highlights the need for harmonized guidelines and further research to optimize their use in routine practice.

papers.title: Neotenic expansion of adult-born dentate granule cells reconfigures GABAergic inhibition to enhance social memory consolidation.
papers.abstract: Immature adult-born dentate granule cells (abDGCs) show heightened synaptic and structural plasticity and preferentially contribute to hippocampal-dependent memory. Protracted maturation (neoteny) of abDGCs in higher mammals is posited to offset the decline in adult hippocampal neurogenesis by supporting increased plasticity. Here we found that selective, synchronous expansion of 4-week-old immature, but not 8-week-old mature, mouse abDGCs promotes recruitment of fast-spiking parvalbumin-expressing inhibitory interneurons (INs) in hippocampal CA3 and CA2, increases feed-forward inhibition, decreases social memory interference and enhances social memory consolidation. In vivo local field potential recordings in dorsal CA1 and CA2 revealed increased baseline power, amplitude and duration of sharp-wave ripples, as well as enhanced rate modulation by social experience. Inhibitory neuron-targeted chemogenetic manipulations implicate dorsal CA3 and CA2 INs, including parvalbumin-expressing INs, as necessary and sufficient for social memory consolidation following and sans neotenic expansion of abDGCs, respectively. Our findings suggest that neoteny of abDGCs supports cognition by increasing feed-forward inhibition in DG-CA3 and DG-CA2 and promoting network oscillations that underlie memory consolidation.

papers.title: The hippocampus as a latent diffusion engine for memory, perception and cognitive dysfunction.
papers.abstract: The hippocampus is a central cognitive hub whose dysfunction contributes to most neurodegenerative dementias. Despite extensive knowledge of its anatomy, physiology and circuitry, a unifying account that links hippocampal dynamics to cognition and clinical syndromes remains lacking. Drawing on systems neuroscience and recent advances in generative artificial intelligence, we conceptualize the hippocampus as a latent diffusion engine that compresses sensory, interoceptive and cognitive inputs into low-dimensional representations and regenerates percepts, episodic memories and imagined scenes for cortical integration. Travelling waves of cortico-hippocampal oscillations, aligned with large-scale functional gradients, schedule and structure this generative process and organize distributed neural activity into coherent, semantically grounded constructs. We formalize this proposal as stochastic latent oscillatory diffusion (SLOD), a biologically grounded framework that maps hippocampal-cortical computations onto specific anatomical substrates and dynamical processes. While we do not suggest that the hippocampus implements diffusion algorithms per se, we show that its computations can be decomposed into homologous operations including compression, stochastic exploration, conditioning and reconstruction, whose formal structure closely parallels that of latent diffusion models. Finally, we demonstrate how major neurodegenerative dementias, including the Alzheimer's disease spectrum, dementia with Lewy bodies and frontotemporal dementia, can be understood as selective breakdowns of distinct components of this generative architecture.

papers.title: Microglia mediate motor memory decay through activity-dependent phagocytosis of myelin sheaths.
papers.abstract: Experience-dependent changes in myelination are important for motor learning, with newly generated oligodendrocytes contributing to the formation of new myelin. However, motor memories decay over time and the underlying mechanisms remain largely unexplored. Here we show that motor memory decay is linked to changes in memory-associated myelin sheaths resulting from microglial phagocytosis in mouse brain. Mechanistically, reduced activity of motor memory engram cells lowers oligodendrocyte expression of the 'don't eat me' signal from Cluster of differentiation 47 (CD47), facilitating microglial phagocytosis and driving myelin loss. Knockout of CD47 from motor memory-associated oligodendrocytes increased microglial phagocytosis of myelin sheaths and accelerated the decay of motor memory, whereas overexpression of CD47 showed opposite results. Moreover, microglia phagocytose myelin sheaths and synapses independently. Our findings reveal that microglial phagocytosis of motor memory-associated myelin sheaths leads to the decay of motor memory. Since various types of memory require myelination in the brain, this mechanism may contribute to the decay of other memory types.

papers.title: A cell-type-resolved proteomic atlas reveals intra- and intercellular signaling in Alzheimer's disease.
papers.abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) arises from pathological interactions among diverse brain cell types, but cell-type-specific proteomic changes remain underexplored. Here, we present deep proteomic profiling of sorted or proximity-labeled brain cells from AD mouse models (5xFAD and AppNL-G-F) at multiple ages, quantifying 13,411 proteins in microglia, astrocytes, oligodendrocyte precursor cells, and neurons, with additional spatial information. We identified 3,028 differentially abundant proteins, most of which were absent in a bulk proteomic dataset, and constructed cell-type-specific networks to define functional modules and hub proteins. Comparison with transcriptomic data revealed that ∼30% of proteomic changes are RNA discordant. Further analyses uncovered cross-cell-type signaling proteins conserved in human AD brains, such as pleiotrophin (Ptn), which is transcriptionally enriched in astrocytes but accumulates in microglia. Importantly, recombinant PTN activates human induced microglia (iMG) cells. Thus, these findings provide a comprehensive cell-type-resolved proteomic atlas of AD models, highlighting novel intra- and intercellular signaling events.

papers.title: Chronic and subacute phenylalanine effects on brain metabolism in adults with phenylketonuria.
papers.abstract: Phenylketonuria (PKU) leads to chronic cerebral exposure to elevated phenylalanine (Phe) despite lifelong dietary treatment, yet the neurometabolic consequences in adulthood remain incompletely understood. We investigated whether adults with early-treated PKU exhibit persistent alterations in brain metabolism and whether these metabolites respond dynamically to subacute Phe fluctuations. Adults with early-treated PKU (n=30) and healthy controls (n=59) underwent proton magnetic resonance spectroscopy (1H-MRS), structural and functional brain MRI to evaluate white matter lesion load (T2-weighted images) and cerebral blood flow (arterial spin labeling), as well as cognitive assessments. Patients additionally participated in a randomized, placebo-controlled crossover intervention with four weeks of oral Phe loading to evaluate subacute metabolic responsiveness. Absolute metabolite concentrations were quantified in predominantly white matter tissue, and associations between blood and brain Phe, white matter lesion load, cerebral blood flow, and cognitive performance were examined. At baseline, patients exhibited higher brain Phe and N-acetylaspartate (NAA) levels, alongside reduced myo-inositol, N-acetylaspartylglutamate (NAAG), and total creatine/phosphocreatine compared with controls. Patients with white matter lesions did not differ in blood and brain metabolites from those without. Four weeks of oral Phe loading increased brain Phe and produced a reversible decrease in myo-inositol, whereas NAA, NAAG, and creatine compounds remained unchanged. Blood and brain Phe concentrations were strongly correlated (r=0.83, p<0.001), and their ratio was subject-dependent. No significant associations were observed between metabolite concentrations and regional cerebral blood flow or cognitive performance after correction for multiple comparisons. Adults with early-treated PKU exhibit persistent neurometabolic alterations involving neuronal-glial metabolism, energy buffering, and astrocytic osmolyte regulation. The findings support a trait-state framework, with stable alterations in NAA, NAAG, and creatine compounds reflecting long-standing metabolic changes, superimposed on a dynamically Phe-sensitive astrocytic response indexed by myo-inositol. The absence of strong associations with cerebral perfusion or cognition suggests that these alterations represent upstream biological processes not captured by macroscopic imaging or behavioral measures.

papers.title: Motor system inefficiency as an activity-dependent amplifier of fatigue in multiple sclerosis.
papers.abstract: Multiple sclerosis (MS) fatigue is clinically obvious but mechanistically elusive. It can dominate daily life despite modest disability, stable structural MRI findings, or preserved strength on examination. This Update reviews evidence that an important component of MS fatigue may arise from increased motor-control cost and incomplete recovery after activity. Voluntary muscle activation studies show that some people with MS have incomplete central access to available force, particularly after exertion. Functional imaging studies indicate that apparently preserved movement often depends on expanded recruitment of premotor, cerebellar, striatal, prefrontal, and cingulo-insular systems involved in motor compensation, effort allocation, and body-state monitoring. Metabolic and pathological studies further indicate energetic vulnerability in demyelinated and chronically injured networks, providing biological plausibility for impaired restoration after repeated signalling demands. These findings support a systems framework in which expanded motor-control recruitment may be compensatory when it preserves performance and remains flexible and recoverable, but may amplify MS fatigue when ordinary activity begins from incompletely restored physiological reserve. We outline testable predictions for identifying a motor-cost fatigue phenotype and for designing repeated-measures studies of activity-related fatigue in MS.

papers.title: Distinct prelimbic microcircuits control sensory and affective dimensions of neuropathic pain.
papers.abstract: The microcircuit mechanisms underlying deactivation and altered output of the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC), a common feature of several chronic pain conditions, are poorly understood. Here, using unbiased in vivo longitudinal multiphoton imaging in the mouse prelimbic cortex (PrL), we show that nerve injury induces sensitization of all classes of GABAergic interneurons and a phenotypic switch from unimodal to polymodal responses. Through circuit interrogation, we identified functions for caudal geminal eminence-derived Prox1+ interneurons and revealed that distinct classes of inhibitory and excitatory neurons in the PrL have different functions in promoting neuropathic pain. In addition, we show that the sensory and affective dimensions of neuropathic pain engaged two distinct microcircuits, PV+-Rbp4+ neurons and Prox1+-Cux2+/Ntsr1+ neurons, respectively, to control distinct projection outputs. These findings provide a mechanistic basis for how mPFC guides actions to avoid or overcome pain and how prefrontal deactivation exacerbates neuropathic pain.

papers.title: D4Z4 methylation and genetic modifiers influence severity in a facioscapulohumeral muscular dystrophy kindred.
papers.abstract: One of the earliest systematic descriptions of facioscapulohumeral muscular dystrophy (FSHD) involved a six-generation kindred tracing back to a single ancestor born in 1775 in Lancashire, England, who later emigrated to Utah in the 1850s. First published in 1950, members of this kindred (K1462) have been followed clinically for decades, with DNA samples archived since the 1980s. Despite sharing the same 5-repeat unit (5RU) D4Z4 contraction on a permissive 4qA haplotype, affected individuals show marked variability in age at onset, clinical severity and disease progression, including within sibships. With long-term follow-up and a shared founder mutation, K1462 is a unique resource for identifying modifiers of disease expression in FSHD. We reintroduce K1462, with enrolment extending into the ninth generation, and perform genomic analysis using modern approaches. Inheritance of the 5RU founder allele was confirmed in 139 individuals, and nanopore Cas9-targeted sequencing determined CpG methylation across the contracted D4Z4 array at base-pair resolution. The 5RU allele showed complete penetrance; however, clinical severity and progression varied widely among affected individuals. Longitudinal analysis of blood-derived genomic DNA demonstrated high stability of D4Z4 CpG methylation within individuals, including samples collected up to 38 years apart, indicating long-term maintenance of the epigenetic state. In contrast, D4Z4 methylation levels differed substantially between individuals and showed a strong inverse correlation with clinical severity. Differences in D4Z4 methylation were observed both within and between families, with a modest but consistent parent-of-origin effect. Whole-genome sequencing analysis found no evidence that rare variants in known FSHD2 genes explained this variability. To assess the contribution of common genetic variation, we performed a pedigree-based genome-wide association analysis of D4Z4 methylation levels, identifying a single genome-wide significant locus on chromosome 15. Variants spanning the promoter and 5' region of HDGFL3, which encodes a PWWP domain chromatin-interacting protein, were associated with increased D4Z4 methylation after accounting for parental transmission, supporting a role for common-variant modulation of methylation in FSHD. These results support a model in which D4Z4 methylation is established through transmission-associated epigenetic resetting, stably maintained within individuals, and quantitatively modified by inherited genetic variation. Together, these findings demonstrate that D4Z4 methylation is a stable, individual-level epigenetic feature that varies across a multigenerational pedigree in a manner that correlates with clinical severity, confirming D4Z4 methylation as a quantitative biomarker and genetically modifiable contributor to disease severity in FSHD.

papers.title: Noncoding functions of FMR1 transcript in riboregulation of human neurodevelopment.
papers.abstract: The noncoding functions of protein-coding messenger RNAs (mRNAs) are largely ignored. Here, we demonstrate an unexpected noncoding role of FMR1 mRNA in human neurodevelopment. A loss of FMR1 and its protein product, fragile X messenger ribonucleoprotein (FMRP), leads to the neurodevelopmental disorder fragile X syndrome (FXS). Neurons derived from FXS patients display hyperexcitability and immature morphology, whereas FMRP knockout (FMRP-KO) neurons that retain FMR1 transcript expression do not. Multi-omics analyses reveal key metabolic differences between FXS and FMRP-KO neurons. Although both FXS and FMRP-KO neurons exhibit reduced mitochondrial respiration, only FXS neurons exhibit elevated glycolysis. We further discover that the FMR1 transcript riboregulates the levels of the glycolytic enzyme lactate dehydrogenase A (LDHA) by inhibiting the binding of LDHA mRNA to insulin-like growth factor 2 mRNA-binding protein 2 (IGF2BP2). Finally, the FMR1 transcript, independent of FMRP, rescues glycolytic and cellular deficits of FXS neurons. Together, these results suggest that FMR1 is a dual-function RNA in human neurodevelopment.
